### 6.10 Sous Vide Brisket (Richie's Method)

**Cody's second brisket, dictated 2026-09-08 — and the credit belongs to Richie.** Richie is Cody's friend and **the founder of Q39**, a famous barbecue place, and this is **his method**, passed along and then cooked Cody's way. **Richie's own verdict on it is the reason it's in this cookbook: he says it tastes pretty much the same as his championship brisket.** That is an unusual thing for a competition pitmaster to say about a water bath, and it's the headline here.

**The shape of it:** coat the brisket **heavily in homemade smoked salt** ([§4.195](4195-codys-smoked-salt.md)) and **a whole bunch of pepper** — a Dalmatian rub, salt and pepper, maybe a hint of garlic, and nothing more. **Separate the point from the flat** so the pieces fit the bags, **put butter in the bag**, and **vacuum it down as hard as the sealer will pull.** Then **150°F for two days straight.** Out of the bath, **the whole bag goes into an ice chest full of ice overnight** to get it cold. The next day: **225°F for about four hours** over a palmful of pecan for a semi-decent bark, and then **the Egg roaring hot for a hot browning — not a sear** — turning it about a minute at a time until the outside is chewy. **Save the juice out of the bag**, warm it in a pan, and spoon a little over the slices as you cut.

> ⚖️ **The honest tradeoff, and Cody names it himself: this method sacrifices some bark, and buys juiciness and control.** A brisket that spent two days at 150°F and then only four hours in smoke will not build the crust that [§6.1 Smoked Brisket](61-smoked-brisket.md)'s twelve-hour straight smoke builds — that's the price. **What you get for it is the thing [§6.1](61-smoked-brisket.md) can't give him: you know exactly when it will be done, and — in his words — *"you never mess it up."*** The bath holds a temperature for two days without help; the four-hour smoke is on your clock, not the meat's; the browning is a few minutes at the end. **Where the smoke flavor comes from is worth understanding, because it isn't only the fire.** It comes from **two places: the four-hour smoke, and the smoked salt that sat on the meat inside a sealed bag for two days.** That's why the salt is not a garnish in this recipe — it's half the smoke.

> **Read this alongside [§6.1](61-smoked-brisket.md), not instead of it.** Two briskets, both Cody's, and they answer different questions. **[§6.1](61-smoked-brisket.md) is the better bark and the unpredictable finish; [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) is the chewy-but-lesser bark and the finish you can schedule.** Neither replaces the other, and neither is a compromise version of the other.

**❤️ Family favorite** — *rated by Cody on 2026-09-09, in a batch of family verdicts given without a per-dish quote.*

> **Why 🟢 Easy — and why this one was Easy even while [§3 Darcy's Steak](3-darcys-steak.md) sat at 🟡** *(it is 🟢 too since 2026-09-09, on Cody's call — the difference below still describes the physics)*. [CLAUDE.md §3a](../../CLAUDE.md)'s test: *can a step go from perfect to ruined?* **Cody answers it himself — *"you never mess it up"* — and walking the steps confirms it.** Two days in a 150°F bath cannot fail; that's the most forgiving stretch of cooking in this book. An overnight in an ice chest cannot fail. A four-hour smoke at 225°F on already-cooked meat cannot fail. **That leaves the hot browning, and it is genuinely lower-risk than a steak sear**, which is the distinction worth drawing: [§3 Darcy's Steak](3-darcys-steak.md) rated 🟡 because **there is doneness left to lose there** — a few seconds too long over a chimney pushes a medium-rare steak past medium rare with no way back. **A brisket that has been at 150°F for two days has no doneness left to lose.** It cannot be overcooked into the wrong doneness; the only thing you can hurt is the crust, by walking away and letting it char — and Cody's own instruction, *turn it about every minute*, is exactly the guard against that. That's a **don't-walk-away caution, not a technique risk.** **And the elapsed time — three days — is Slow cook and lead time, which per [§1 Cody's Pho](1-codys-pho.md) never inflates a rating.** Three days of waiting, about fifty minutes of work.

> ⚠️ **Dry seasoning only in the bag — no fresh garlic, no liquid.** This cookbook's established anaerobic-bag rule from [§1 Cody's Pho](1-codys-pho.md) applies here exactly as written, and at 150°F for **two days** it matters more than usual, not less: raw garlic sealed in an oxygen-free bag at sub-boiling temperature is a botulism setup, and **garlic powder is the safe substitute** — which is what the "hint of garlic" in the Dalmatian rub should be. Salt, pepper, garlic powder, and butter are what belong in this bag. *(Butter is a fat, not a liquid marinade, and it's Richie's — see Step 4.)*

> 🌡️ **On 150°F for 48 hours, from [§T44](t44-food-safety--the-real-logic-and-the-target-temperature-table.md) rather than from Cody.** This is well **above** this cookbook's danger zone, so the long hold is not a food-safety question the way a 125°F bath would be — 150°F pasteurizes, and two days at it is what turns brisket's connective tissue to gelatin without the temperature ever climbing past it. **It is also a different target from this book's other sous vide numbers, on purpose:** [§6 Established Kitchen Facts](../../CLAUDE.md) records **131–133°F for 24–48 hours** for Cody's sous vide beef, and [§T27](t27-sous-vide-not-so-premium-steak-cuts-codys-method.md) runs around 129°F — those are *steak* temperatures, aimed at medium rare. **Brisket is not steak**, and 150°F is a barbecue temperature aimed at melting collagen. Both numbers are his and neither corrects the other. **(All temperatures in this cookbook are °F.)**

#### A. Ingredients

- **1 packer brisket** — the whole thing, point and flat together, so you can separate them yourself *(Cody didn't name a size or grade; [§T69](t69-brisket-basics--anatomy-of-a-whole-packer-brisket.md)'s buying rule applies — **8 to 16 lb, USDA Choice, Prime or Wagyu, handpicked for marbling.** See Open Questions)*
- **[§4.195 Cody's Smoked Salt](4195-codys-smoked-salt.md)** — **heavily. Go heavier than feels right**, because **a lot of the salt cooks out over two days.** Coarse smoked sea salt is what he uses; he smokes pink Himalayan too
- **Coarse ground black pepper** — **a whole bunch of it.** With the salt, this is the **Dalmatian rub** ([§4.105](4105-dalmatian-rub.md)) — and that's the whole seasoning
- **Garlic powder** — *maybe a hint*, optional. **Powder, not fresh** — see the bag warning above
- **Butter** — **into the bag with the meat** *(Cody didn't give an amount; see Open Questions)*
- **Smoking wood — pecan.** **A palm-sized chunk, a handful, no more** ([§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md)). **Pecan is his favorite; hickory does great too**
- **Ice** — **enough to fill an ice chest** around the bags, for the overnight chill *(Step 6)*
- **Avocado oil** — only if you're making the **burnt ends** in Section D

*Not groceries, but this recipe doesn't happen without them: a **sous vide circulator** big enough to run for two days, a **vacuum sealer** — Cody's is commercial-grade and it matters here (Step 5) — **bags** large enough for half a brisket, an **ice chest**, a **smoker or kamado**, and a **pan** for warming the juice.*

#### B. Cooking Instructions

**1. Break the packer down — separate the point from the flat.**
**This is a bag-fitting problem before it's anything else:** a whole packer will not go into a vacuum bag, so it comes apart first. **Separating the two muscles is easier than it sounds, because the brisket does most of the work for you.** Look at the side of the brisket and find the **thick layer of fat that runs between the point and the flat** — that fat seam is the seam you're cutting. Slide a long knife into it and follow it, keeping the blade angled toward the fat rather than into either muscle; **once you get the cut started you can very often just pull the two apart with your hands.** Trim off the excess surface fat and any silverskin while the pieces are open. *(The flat is the long lean one, ¼ inch to about 1½ inches thick; the point is the thick oval that sits on top of one end of it, more than 4 inches thick — [§T69 Brisket Basics](t69-brisket-basics--anatomy-of-a-whole-packer-brisket.md) has the anatomy.)*

> 📖 **Cookbook judgment, labeled — where the separation technique comes from.** **Cody said to look this one up**, so per [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md) it was looked up here first, and this cookbook already answered it twice from a named source. **The technique above is Meathead Goldwyn's**, from ***The Meathead Method***'s Championship Brisket — transcribed in this cookbook at [§7.135](7135-championship-brisket-and-burnt-ends.md), which separates the point and flat before cooking in exactly these words: *follow the fat layer between them with your knife, and once you get a cut started you can often just tear them apart with your hands.* [§T70 Slicing Brisket](t70-slicing-brisket--the-easy-way-vs-the-sorkin-way.md) (same author) describes the same seam from the carving side — *slide your knife between the two muscles and cut out that thick triangular lump of excess fat* — and [§T69](t69-brisket-basics--anatomy-of-a-whole-packer-brisket.md) supplies the anatomy. **The method, the reason for doing it, and the against-the-grain rule below are Cody's; the description of how to make the cut is the cookbook's, from Meathead. His own account of how he does it supersedes this the day he gives it.**

**2. If the pieces still won't fit the bags, cut them down — as large as will fit, and ACROSS THE GRAIN.**
The point and flat may still be too big for your bags. **Cut them into the largest chunks that will fit — not convenient small ones.** Bigger pieces hold more juice and give you longer, better slices at the end. **And make every one of those cuts across the grain**, because the direction you cut now decides how the meat eats later: **the grain of the flat and the grain of the point run different ways**, so once they're apart, read each muscle separately and cut perpendicular to its own fibers. Getting this wrong is the one mistake in this recipe that can't be fixed afterward — a beautifully cooked brisket sliced with the grain still chews like a rope. *(A trick worth borrowing from [§7.112](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md): before it goes in the bag, notch a corner or stick a toothpick in parallel to the grain, so you can still find it two days later.)*

**3. Season it heavily — smoked salt and a whole bunch of pepper. Go heavier than feels right.**
**Coat every surface heavily in [§4.195 Cody's Smoked Salt](4195-codys-smoked-salt.md)**, then **a whole bunch of coarse black pepper**, and a hint of **garlic powder** if you want it. That's the entire seasoning — **a Dalmatian rub** ([§4.105](4105-dalmatian-rub.md)), and Cody's instruction is to keep it simple. **The part that will feel wrong is the amount of salt, and it is deliberate:** ***a lot of the salt cooks out over the two days***, dissolving into the juice that the meat releases into the bag, so a normal hand with the salt lands underseasoned two days later. Go heavier than you would on a brisket you were about to smoke. *(This is the same instinct as [§T37](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md)'s heavy-every-time dry brine, with a second reason on top of it. And note that the smoked salt is doing double duty here — it's the seasoning **and** it's half the smoke flavor in the finished brisket, since it sits sealed against the meat for 48 hours.)*

**4. Butter in the bag, then bag it.**
**A piece of butter goes into the bag with the meat** — Richie's method, and it's what the meat sits in for two days alongside its own juices. Put the seasoned meat in the bag with the butter and nothing else. **No liquid, no fresh garlic** — see the warning above.

**5. Vacuum it as hard as your sealer will pull. Then check it again.**
**Start as tight as the machine can possibly get it.** This is Cody's own reasoning and it's specific to a two-day cook: **the bag loosens as the meat releases juice.** What comes out of the meat over 48 hours has to go somewhere, and it goes into the bag — so a seal that looked snug on day one is slack by day two, and a slack bag floats, insulates, and stops making even contact with the water. Pull it down as hard as you can at the start and you have margin to lose. *(Cody uses a **commercial-grade vacuum sealer**; a home sealer will do this, it just won't pull as hard, so check the bags the next morning and re-seal anything that has gone loose or is floating.)*

**6. 150°F for two days. Straight.**
Set the bath to **150°F** and leave it for **48 hours.** That's the whole step — it is the most hands-off thing in this book, and it is where the brisket actually becomes brisket: two days at 150°F is long enough to melt the collagen that makes this cut tough, at a temperature far below anything that would squeeze the meat dry. **Nothing needs turning, checking, or adjusting.** Keep the water topped up and covered if your rig loses much to evaporation over two days, and keep the bags submerged.

**7. The whole bag into an ice chest full of ice. Overnight.**
Out of the bath, **the bags go straight into an ice chest packed with ice** and stay there **overnight**, until the meat is cold all the way through. **Do not open the bags.** This does two jobs. **It gets the brisket out of the danger zone fast** and parks it cold until you're ready — which is a large part of how this method hands you control over the schedule. **And it sets up the smoke**: cold meat takes smoke better than warm meat does, a point Meathead makes directly in [§7.131 Smoked Sous-Vide Steak](7131-smoked-sous-vide-steak.md) — *cold, wet meat attracts and holds smoke* — which is the same bath → ice → smoke → sear sequence this recipe runs, at brisket scale. **⚠️ This cooler has ICE in it.** So does [§3 Darcy's Steak](3-darcys-steak.md)'s, for the same reason — chill a bagged sous vide cut down hard before it meets fire. **It is the opposite of [§6.9 Cody's Pulled Pork](69-codys-pulled-pork.md)'s cooler, which has no ice at all and is holding heat in.** Same equipment, opposite jobs; don't mix them up.

**8. Smoke it at 225°F for about four hours, over a palmful of pecan.**
Bring the smoker to **225°F**, put **a handful — a palm-sized chunk — of pecan** on the fire, wait for the smoke to go **thin and blue** rather than white ([§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md); the bitter smoke burns off first, and [§6.1](61-smoked-brisket.md) Step 4 has the full version of this), and put the cold brisket on. **About four hours.** **Pecan is his favorite; hickory does great too.** **What you are after here is bark, not doneness** — the meat has been cooked for two days already, and nothing in these four hours is trying to raise its internal temperature to a target. In Cody's words it gets you a **semi-decent bark**, which is an honest description: four hours builds a real crust and real smoke flavor, and it does not build the crust that twelve hours of straight smoke builds. **Go light on the wood** — a palmful, per his standing rule — because four hours of smoke on a cold, damp surface takes on plenty.

**9. Then get the Egg roaring hot and give it a HOT BROWNING — not a sear. Turn it about every minute, until the outside is chewy.**
This is the finish and the words matter: **a hot browning, not a sear.** Open the Egg up and **get it roaring hot**, then put the brisket on and **keep turning it, about a minute at a time**, working the whole outside. **You are not trying to put a steakhouse crust on one face — you're drying and firming the entire exterior into something with chew.** Cody is specific about the target: ***"a nice, salty, smoky chewy bark."*** That's the sensory checkpoint — pick it up and look at it, and stop when the outside has gone dark, dry to the touch and genuinely chewy rather than soft. **Don't walk away.** There is no doneness left to lose in this brisket, so the only thing a hot fire can take from you is the crust, and a minute of inattention over a roaring fire is how it goes from chewy to charred.

**10. Save the juice from the bag. Warm it in a pan and spoon it over the slices as you cut.**
**Do not pour the bag out.** Two days at 150°F leaves a serious amount of rendered, salty, buttery, smoke-seasoned liquid in there, and **it is the best thing in this recipe.** Pour it into a pan and **warm it gently** — don't boil it down, you're not making a sauce — and then **slice the brisket and spoon a little over the slices as you cut.** Slice **across the grain** of whichever muscle you're cutting ([§T70](t70-slicing-brisket--the-easy-way-vs-the-sorkin-way.md); the toothpick from Step 2 is telling you where the grain runs), and cut at the last minute — brisket dries fast once it's open, which is exactly what the warm juice is there to answer. **Taste the juice before you use it**; it can be salty on its own, which is a good reason to spoon rather than pour.

**Cody didn't name a weight**, so this runs on a **12 lb untrimmed packer**, the same assumed size as [§6.1 Smoked Brisket](61-smoked-brisket.md) and [§7.112 Texas Beef Brisket](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md), so all three brisket entries stay comparable. **The butter is estimated at about 4 Tbsp across the bags**, since no amount was given — that assumption is labeled here and flagged in Open Questions. Scale linearly for a different brisket. *(Estimated per [CLAUDE.md §3b](../../CLAUDE.md).)*

| | Calories | Fat | Protein | Carbs | Fiber |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Whole dish** *(a 12 lb packer + butter, as eaten)* | ~9,400 | 665 g | 720 g | 2 g | 1 g |
| **Per serving** *(serves 12)* | ~785 | 55 g | 60 g | 0.2 g | 0.1 g |

**What a serving is:** about **6 to 7 oz of sliced brisket**, mixing lean flat and rich point, with a spoonful of the warmed bag juice over it — a dinner plate's worth of meat, or a big sandwich.

**How these were figured.** From the ingredient list, not lab figures, and **counting only what's eaten.** **A sous vide brisket keeps more of itself than a smoked one does** — less fat renders away over two days at 150°F than over twelve hours at 225°F, and a good deal of what does come out is spooned back over the meat as juice in Step 10 rather than dripping into a pit — so the yield here runs a little higher and a little richer per ounce than [§6.1](61-smoked-brisket.md)'s. **The butter is counted** (~400 calories, ~45 g fat across the whole dish) because it ends up in the juice and the juice goes on the plate. **The salt and pepper are the entire carb and fiber column** and they are nearly nothing. **If you make the burnt ends in Section D**, they come out of this same brisket rather than in addition to it — count them from Section D's own block instead of double-counting the point here.

#### D. Burnt Ends — Cody's, from the Point

**Burnt ends made from the point after the four-hour smoke, cubed, oiled and crisped in a pan.** They are a section of this recipe rather than a recipe of their own, for the same reason [§7.51's Fried Boudin Patties](751-boudin-blanc-boudin.md#d-variation--fried-boudin-patties) are: **they cannot be made without the brisket above** — the whole ingredient list is *the point of [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md), plus oil and sauce.*

> 🦆 **Where this came from, and Cody's line about it.** [§T71 Burnt Ends](t71-burnt-ends.md) records Meathead's own aside: he's been known to crisp burnt ends in a frying pan with **bacon fat or duck fat** — and that ***"will get you disqualified at a competition, but not at the dinner table."*** **Cody's answer to that is the whole spirit of this entry:** ***"I'm not in a competition. I'm in it for taste."*** **So this is his combination of two things** — **Richie's sous vide brisket** above, and **the fried-burnt-end idea from Meathead** — **with avocado oil in place of the duck fat.** *(Avocado oil is the same choice he makes at [§3 Darcy's Steak](3-darcys-steak.md) Step 6, and for the same reason: it holds above 500°F where olive oil would burn.)*

**🟢 Easy** · **Prep ~10 min** *(cubing the point and oiling it)* · **Cook ~10 min** *(a pan sear, in batches)* · **Start to finish ~20 min** *(starting from the smoked point of [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) above — everything before that is that recipe's time, not this section's)*

##### Ingredients

- **The point** from [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) above, **after the four-hour smoke** *(Step 8)*
- **Avocado oil** — enough to **drizzle a light, greasy layer** over the cubes. **Not heavy**
- **Your favorite barbecue sauce** — for the side, or drizzled over half *(this cookbook's own house options: [§4.117 Kansas City Classic](4117-kansas-city-classic-barbecue-sauce.md), [§4.118 Columbia Gold](4118-columbia-gold-south-carolina-mustard-sauce.md))*

##### Cooking Instructions

**1. Cube the point.**
**Burnt ends come from the point, not the flat**, and there's a reason beyond tradition: the point is the fattier, thicker, more uneven of the two muscles, which makes it hard to slice attractively and ideal to cube — the extra fat is what makes a burnt end lush instead of dry ([§T71](t71-burnt-ends.md)). **Cut it into bite-sized cubes** — [§T71](t71-burnt-ends.md)'s figure is about ¾ inch, and [§7.135](7135-championship-brisket-and-burnt-ends.md)'s is ¾ to 1 inch, both from the same author; Cody just says cube it up.

**2. Drizzle with avocado oil — a light greasy layer, not a heavy one.**
**Drizzle or spray avocado oil over the cubes and toss them so every side has a sheen.** Cody's description is exact and worth keeping: **a nice greasy layer, not heavy.** You are giving the pan something to fry against, not deep-frying anything.

**3. Pan sear, just to crisp the outside — about a minute a side. DO NOT COOK IT THROUGH.**
Get a pan hot, lay the cubes in **in a single layer with space between them**, and **sear just until the outsides crisp and darken** — turning them so several faces get color, roughly a minute a face. **This is a pan sear, not a fry, and the meat is already cooked** — it has been through two days of sous vide and four hours of smoke. **Cooking it through is the only way to ruin it**; the pan is there to crisp an exterior, and the moment the cubes have crunchy faces they come out. **Work in batches** if the pan is crowded — crowded cubes steam instead of crisping.

**4. Serve on a board, with sauce on the side or over half.**
Pile them on a cutting board and serve with **your favorite barbecue sauce on the side, or drizzled over half of them** — half sauced and half bare is Cody's own way to put it out, and it's a good instinct: these are salty, smoky and rich on their own, and not everyone wants sauce on top of that.

##### Grocery Shopping List

**🛒 General grocery**

- 🛒 Avocado oil *(already on [§6.10's list](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) above)*
- 🛒 Barbecue sauce — your favorite *(or make one: [§4.117](4117-kansas-city-classic-barbecue-sauce.md), [§4.118](4118-columbia-gold-south-carolina-mustard-sauce.md))*

*The meat is already in the kitchen — this section buys almost nothing.*

#### Nutrition *(estimated — Burnt Ends)*

| | Calories | Fat | Protein | Carbs | Fiber |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **The whole point, cubed** *(~2½ lb as eaten, from a 12 lb packer)* | ~3,400 | 275 g | 215 g | 12 g | 0.4 g |
| **Per serving** *(serves 8 as an appetizer)* | ~425 | 34 g | 27 g | 1.5 g | 0.1 g |

**What a serving is:** about **5 oz — five or six cubes**, a few off a shared board, with a spoon of sauce. As a main course rather than a passed appetizer, figure half as many servings and double the numbers.

**How these were figured.** The point is the fatty muscle, so these run richer per ounce than the sliced-brisket figures above — that's the whole appeal of a burnt end. **The avocado oil is counted at about 2 Tbsp for the batch** (most of it stays on the meat, which is the point of a light layer) and **the barbecue sauce at about 2 Tbsp per serving**, which is where the small carb number comes from — leave it off and the carbs go to zero. **⚠️ These cubes come out of the same brisket as the block above, not in addition to it** — if you make burnt ends, count them here and take a serving or two off §6.10's count.

#### E. Open Questions

- **What size brisket, and what grade?** No weight, packer size or grade was given for this method either. The entry runs on [§T69](t69-brisket-basics--anatomy-of-a-whole-packer-brisket.md)'s buying rule and prices its Nutrition on an assumed 12 lb packer, both labeled. **His own answer replaces both.**
- **How much butter goes in the bag?** He said butter, not how much. The Nutrition block assumes about **4 Tbsp across the bags** and says so; a real figure from him would close it. *(Also unrecorded: salted or unsalted — which matters more than usual here, given how heavily the meat is already salted.)*
- **Is the ice-chest chill always overnight, or is that just how his schedule falls?** Written as overnight because that's how he described it. Whether a shorter hard chill would do, and whether the bags can go to the fridge after the ice chest and wait a day or two before the smoke, isn't recorded — though [§7.131](7131-smoked-sous-vide-steak.md) does exactly that with a steak.
- **How long is the hot browning, in total?** He gave the cadence — **turning it about a minute at a time** — but not how many turns or how many minutes overall. Step 9 goes by the look and feel of the bark instead. His number would be better.
- **Does he rest it after the browning?** Not stated. There is an argument that it doesn't need one *([§T33](t33-how-meat-actually-cooks--conduction-carryover-and-why-resting-is-a-myth.md) — the meat has been at temperature for days and the browning was minutes)*, but that's reasoning, not his answer.
- **Are the point and flat treated differently in the bath?** They're very different thicknesses, and [§7.135](7135-championship-brisket-and-burnt-ends.md) pulls them at different temperatures when smoking. In a fixed-temperature bath that concern mostly disappears — but whether Cody bags them separately, for how long each, and whether the flat comes out earlier, isn't recorded.
- **How does he warm the juice, and does he skim it?** Step 10 says warm it gently in a pan, which is what he described. Whether he strains the solids or skims the fat off first isn't recorded; [§7.135](7135-championship-brisket-and-burnt-ends.md) sieves its foil liquid before serving it.
- **🚫 No ❤️ family-favorite rating on this entry, deliberately.** The **❤️ *"Awesome"*** on [§6.1 Smoked Brisket](61-smoked-brisket.md) was given against **that** entry — the straight smoke — when the section was rated, and it hasn't been given to this method. **Nothing is being inferred from it here.** Richie's verdict is recorded because Richie gave it; Cody's own rating of this specific method is simply not on the record yet.
